weeks.applicationTask: Develop a three-option community recreation decision matrix with full estimated cost, schedule, transport, physical and communication access, weather/safety, information still to verify and a no-cost or no-travel backup. Calculate one weekly cost scenario and defend a feasible, inclusive choice.

weeks.title: Independent practice
weeks.essentialQuestion: How can a learner plan, self-monitor, document and revise independent practice that is safe, feasible and aligned with a clearly stated movement-skill goal?
weeks.scenario: A fictional Grade 9 learner wants to independently practice an eight-count rhythm and controlled wall-press technique. They have two short time windows, variable energy and limited equipment. Their first plan says 'practice hard every day until perfect' but contains no cue, recovery, evidence or stop rule. Redesign it so practice remains voluntary, measurable, accessible and realistic.
weeks.model: Worked independent practice plan: Goal—explain or perform an eight-count rhythm with a steady pace. Preparation—check space and comfortable support. Optional attempt—work through one manageable sequence, pause and note whether counts 1–8 were clear; repeat only if comfortable. Alternative—tap the rhythm seated or annotate a fictional demonstration. Self-check—identify one accurate element and one improvement. Stop if uncomfortable or unwell; record a decision and review next time. No forced duration, intensity or personal health disclosure.

days.concept: Independent work begins with a controllable process goal, not a promise about appearance or pushing harder. A good plan states the skill, available setting, evidence and when to review.
days.instruction: Independent work begins with a controllable process goal, not a promise about appearance or pushing harder. A good plan states the skill, available setting, evidence and when to review.
days.practice: Compare an unsafe daily repetition quota with a goal to explain or show an eight-count sequence while checking timing and comfort.
days.workedExample: 'Practice until perfect' provides no observable success measure; 'identify correct counts and one improvement' can be evaluated.
days.independentTask: Write one skill-based goal, two success cues and a realistic optional practice window.
days.evidence: Specific process goal, relevant cues and feasible access choice.
days.successCriteria: I can choose an independent learning goal I can evaluate safely.

days.concept: Preparation includes checking space and support, deciding on a gentle familiar task, preparing an accessible option and planning recovery. A written plan may be more appropriate than movement in unsafe circumstances.
days.instruction: Preparation includes checking space and support, deciding on a gentle familiar task, preparing an accessible option and planning recovery. A written plan may be more appropriate than movement in unsafe circumstances.
days.practice: Model a brief optional step-touch or seated rhythm sequence: scan surroundings, move comfortably, count the pattern, pause and reflect.
days.workedExample: A learner finds the floor cluttered and chooses a seated tap or annotated video description instead; the planning objective is still met.
days.independentTask: Construct a five-step practice card covering setup, movement/analysis, cues, stop rule and a seated or written alternative.
days.evidence: Complete safe setup, realistic sequence, explicit stop decision and accessible equivalent.
days.successCriteria: I can organize independent practice without relying on high demands or specialized gear.

days.concept: Self-monitoring means gathering task-related observations, not diagnosing health. Useful evidence includes stable support, controlled timing, successful identification of a cue or an accurately explained correction. Keep records brief and private.
days.instruction: Self-monitoring means gathering task-related observations, not diagnosing health. Useful evidence includes stable support, controlled timing, successful identification of a cue or an accurately explained correction. Keep records brief and private.
days.practice: Fill a two-entry fictional log, noting observed rhythm counts, environmental context, pauses and corrections; distinguish observation from inference.
days.workedExample: 'I identified counts 1–8 correctly after slowing down' supports rhythm understanding; 'my cardiovascular fitness improved' does not follow.
days.independentTask: Write two short practice or analysis entries with what happened, context, two cues and one limitation.
days.evidence: Specific relevant observations, clear limits and privacy-safe documentation.
days.successCriteria: I can collect useful evidence while avoiding unsupported fitness conclusions.

days.studentTitle: Revise practice from feedback and recovery
days.concept: Practice adjustments should respond to the evidence and conditions. A learner may keep difficulty stable, shorten an activity, change modality, ask a teacher or choose rest rather than automatically increasing demand.
days.instruction: Practice adjustments should respond to the evidence and conditions. A learner may keep difficulty stable, shorten an activity, change modality, ask a teacher or choose rest rather than automatically increasing demand.
days.practice: Compare fictional attempts with rushed movement and a later controlled attempt. Determine whether the evidence supports repeating, adapting or pausing.
days.workedExample: A controlled seated sequence with accurate counts meets the timing objective more clearly than an extended attempt with repeated errors.
days.independentTask: Rewrite an inflexible 'add more every day' plan with one specific correction, a recovery option and a review question.
days.evidence: Reasoned adjustment based on recorded cues and safety rather than intensity.
days.successCriteria: I can use feedback and recovery needs to improve my practice choices.

days.concept: An effective final portfolio links objective, feasible actions, observations, accessible paths, stop choices and a justified next step. Written evidence of skill understanding and direct motor performance must be labeled accurately.
days.instruction: An effective final portfolio links objective, feasible actions, observations, accessible paths, stop choices and a justified next step. Written evidence of skill understanding and direct motor performance must be labeled accurately.
days.practice: Present the modeled eight-count plan, two observations and revision, explaining what was actually demonstrated versus only analyzed.
days.workedExample: The student can defend why a shorter controlled attempt or a diagrammed alternative better serves the learning target than forced repetitions.
days.independentTask: Submit a two-opportunity portfolio with goal, preparation, technique criteria, evidence, feedback, accessibility choice and revision.
days.evidence: Complete aligned portfolio, honest evidence labeling, safety, self-reflection and justified future plan.
days.successCriteria: I can manage and explain an independent practice cycle based on evidence and choice.

weeks.misconception: Independent practice means training alone without limits and increasing repetitions or intensity each time.
weeks.correction: Responsible independent practice uses an attainable skill goal, safe setup, relevant observations, appropriate support and recovery, plus justified adjustments rather than mandatory escalation.
weeks.teacherNotes: Independent does not mean unsupervised hazardous exercise. Permit seated, diagrammed, narrated and fictional-record options. Never require body metrics, private health disclosure, home exercise proof or maximum repetitions. Score reasoning and appropriate evidence; document directly observed movement separately.

checks.prompt: During independent practice, which plan best applies the week's focus skill: explain how to choose and self-monitor a feasible session?
options: Choose the hardest version regardless of conditions.
Practice the focus skill in a feasible task, explain the choice, and record observable evidence.
Record only whether the task was finished, without explaining the decision.
checks.rationale: The learner applies explain how to choose and self-monitor a feasible session by making a feasible, justified choice and pointing to evidence relevant to independent practice.

checks.prompt: A learner has limited time and no specialized equipment while preparing for independent practice. Which next step best supports this week's learning?
options: Copy a classmate's decision without checking the case.
Identify the decision, compare realistic options, and explain the choice using the learning target.
Use completion time as the only measure of learning.
checks.rationale: A contextual decision responds to the actual constraints and makes its reasoning visible; speed or copying is insufficient.

checks.prompt: Which observation gives the strongest evidence of progress on the focus skill "explain how to choose and self-monitor a feasible session"?
options: A general statement that the learner looked more athletic.
A single score with no description of the task or conditions.
A dated before-and-after observation tied to a clear criterion, with limits noted.
checks.rationale: Relevant, dated evidence tied to a criterion supports a defensible conclusion better than appearance or an unexplained score.

checks.prompt: A peer says, "More intensity or outperforming classmates always means better learning about independent practice." Which response best corrects the reasoning?
options: Treat effort or peer comparison as the main evidence, even when task conditions differ.
Keep the claim without checking the observation, adaptation, or learning objective.
Learning is evaluated by informed choices, safe technique, explanation, reflection and documented progress relative to a learner's own context.
checks.rationale: The correction prioritizes learning evidence and avoids unsupported comparisons or unsafe generalizations.

checks.prompt: The current plan for independent practice is missing a clear success criterion. What revision is most useful?
options: Name one observable criterion for "explain how to choose and self-monitor a feasible session", then record what happened and what remains uncertain.
Add more activity without deciding what will be observed.
Judge success by effort alone and omit the learning evidence.
checks.rationale: A clear criterion connects the activity to observable evidence and acknowledges uncertainty.

checks.prompt: What is independent practice?
options: Doing a task without any safety consideration.
Planning and carrying out an appropriate task while monitoring choices and evidence.
Always training alone without guidance.
checks.rationale: Independent practice includes planning and self-monitoring, not the absence of support.

checks.prompt: Which plan is appropriate for a learner practicing independently for the first time?
options: Choose a familiar, manageable activity, clear space, and a plan for stopping or asking for help.
Try an unfamiliar maximal challenge in an isolated place.
Ignore instructions because the activity is independent.
checks.rationale: A safe first plan matches experience and includes appropriate support.

checks.prompt: What should a learner check before beginning an independent session?
options: Goal, space, equipment, comfort, time, and stop cues.
Only the number of repetitions.
Whether someone else is doing a harder session.
checks.rationale: Independent planning still requires the normal safety and context checks.

checks.prompt: A learner discovers the planned equipment is missing. What should happen?
options: Abandon all reflection.
Improvise with an unstable object.
Use a safe alternative that meets the objective, or postpone the task.
checks.rationale: A substitution should be appropriate to the goal and safe to use.

checks.prompt: Which is an example of self-monitoring?
options: Use only a classmate's opinion.
Ignore symptoms to finish the plan.
Notice effort or comfort, check the plan, and adapt when needed.
checks.rationale: Self-monitoring means checking one's response against the goal and conditions.

checks.prompt: Why include a check-in during independent practice?
options: It allows the learner to review control, comfort, and whether the plan remains suitable.
It guarantees the plan cannot change.
It replaces the need for a goal.
checks.rationale: Check-ins help identify when to continue, adapt, or stop.

checks.prompt: What should a learner do if an independent session feels unsafe?
options: Continue because independence requires finishing.
Stop and seek appropriate help or choose a safer alternative.
Hide the issue.
checks.rationale: Independence includes knowing when to stop or ask for support.

checks.prompt: Which record best documents independent practice?
options: Planned activity, what was attempted, adjustments, and a brief reflection.
A claim of perfect performance without evidence.
A ranking of classmates.
checks.rationale: The record should connect planning and actual decisions.

checks.prompt: A learner has a busy week and cannot complete the plan. What is a useful next step?
options: Double every future session automatically.
Review what was feasible and adjust the schedule or task.
Assume the plan must never change.
checks.rationale: Plans should be revised based on the learner's actual circumstances.

checks.prompt: Which task can show independent planning without physical performance?
options: Write a list of the hardest exercises.
Create a session plan with goal, setup, adaptation, stop cue, and review evidence.
Copy another student's log.
checks.rationale: A detailed plan can demonstrate the reasoning target.

checks.prompt: What is one limit of self-reported activity notes?
options: They always give a complete scientific account.
They may omit details or depend on memory, so conclusions should be cautious.
They can diagnose injuries.
checks.rationale: Self-report is useful evidence but has known limits.

checks.prompt: A learner wants to use an online workout video independently. What should they check?
options: Whether the video promises guaranteed results.
Only view count.
Source, instructions, space, equipment, appropriateness, and whether it allows safe adaptation.
checks.rationale: Online instructions should be checked for credibility and fit before use.

checks.prompt: Why should an independent plan include a stop or help-seeking option?
options: A learner may encounter changing symptoms, equipment, or environmental conditions.
It means the learner is not independent.
It guarantees all risks disappear.
checks.rationale: A safe plan anticipates how to respond to changing conditions.

checks.prompt: A learner uses a seated practice option and records observations. What should the reviewer look for?
options: Whether the evidence addresses the stated learning goal and self-monitoring choices.
Whether the learner matches a standing demonstration.
Whether the learner avoided all adaptations.
checks.rationale: Evaluation should focus on the objective and quality of the learner's decisions.

checks.prompt: Which independent goal is more specific?
options: Complete a chosen 10-minute movement session in a safe space and write one observation afterward.
Get better at everything.
Never need help.
checks.rationale: Specific goals identify an action and a way to review it.

checks.prompt: How should students react when their independent plan needs to change mid-session?
options: Pause, reassess the reason, and document or choose a suitable change.
Continue without thinking because the plan is fixed.
Hide any change from the teacher.
checks.rationale: Adapting in response to evidence is part of responsible independent practice.

checks.prompt: Which helps make independent practice more inclusive?
options: Punish requests for clarification.
Assume independent means every learner uses the same activity.
Provide multiple ways to demonstrate the target and ask for appropriate support when needed.
checks.rationale: Independent practice should not remove reasonable supports or equivalent pathways.

checks.prompt: What is a reasonable role for a teacher in independent practice?
options: Make every decision for the learner.
Require no instructions or support at all.
Set expectations, review evidence, provide feedback, and help with safety or access questions.
checks.rationale: Independence develops within clear boundaries and appropriate support.

checks.prompt: Which is an example of evidence-based revision?
options: I changed every part of the plan without noting a reason.
I moved the session indoors because the outdoor route was unsafe and recorded why.
I followed a suggestion because it was popular.
checks.rationale: Evidence-based revisions connect conditions to a reasoned change.

checks.prompt: Which reflection best evaluates independent practice?
options: Was my performance better than everyone else's?
Did I avoid every break?
Did I plan safely, monitor my response, adapt when needed, and record what I learned?
checks.rationale: The reflection checks planning, monitoring, adaptation, and evidence.

weeks.focusSkill: Explain how to choose and self-monitor a feasible session.
weeks.conceptExplanation: Independent practice is planned skill learning without continuous teacher prompting, not unsupervised high-risk exercise. An effective cycle states one skill target, selects a suitable activity or analysis, checks conditions, practices with relevant cues, records observable evidence, seeks feedback when appropriate and decides whether to repeat, adjust or rest. Self-monitoring cannot diagnose fitness or medical conditions. Brief, controlled attempts and thoughtful observations can demonstrate stronger learning than many unexamined repetitions. A plan should specify when adult supervision or professional assistance is required.
weeks.biomechanicsAndTechnique: Choose familiar low-risk tasks such as a comfortable step-touch rhythm, supported wall press or seated arm pattern; inspect stable surfaces and clear space, move gradually and use controllable range. Do not use heavy loads, extreme balance challenges, risky equipment or unsupervised tasks requiring spotting. Stop for pain, dizziness, unusual symptoms or instability and follow appropriate adult/school assistance procedures. Students can use diagrams, narrated analysis or fictional records when physical performance is unsuitable.
weeks.workedExample: Vague plan: 'Every day do 50 wall presses faster than yesterday.' Revised: 'When a safe practice opportunity is available, complete or analyze a few comfortable wall presses using stable footing and smooth motion. Record whether the two cues were met, identify one correction and choose rest or a seated palm press if appropriate.' This shows independently managed skill learning without implying that more repetitions equal mastery.
weeks.applicationTask: Create a two-opportunity independent practice portfolio with a specific process goal, safe preparation checklist, movement or analysis option, at least two technique cues, two brief observation entries (fictional or optional personal), reflection on evidence, a stop/rest rule, and an adjusted next practice plan. Label planning evidence separately from any directly observed motor demonstration.

weeks.title: Portfolio construction
weeks.essentialQuestion: How can we make a safe, evidence-based decision about portfolio construction?
weeks.scenario: A Grade 9 learner is planning a safe, accessible activity involving portfolio construction. They have limited time, variable energy, and no specialized equipment.
weeks.model: Worked example (portfolio): A learner wants to practice portfolio construction. First identify the specific skill: Select evidence showing revision rather than just performance. Next compare two feasible options, select one with a clear safety cue, and document the reason. A written, observed, seated or adapted demonstration can meet the same reasoning target.

days.instruction: Introduce portfolio construction. Discuss the difference between participation, movement skill and health status. Analyze the case: A Grade 9 learner is planning a safe, accessible activity involving portfolio construction. They have limited time, variable energy, and no specialized equipment.
days.practice: Write a three-part safety plan for portfolio construction: purpose, feasible option, and stop/modification cue.
days.evidence: A reasoned three-part plan with a specific observable cue.

days.instruction: Teacher models one safe approach to portfolio construction and one accessible seated, low-impact, observation or explanation alternative. Compare what each demonstrates.
days.practice: Practice the week's decision with this exact prompt: Select evidence showing revision rather than just performance. Demonstrate it physically when safe, or explain/annotate an equivalent demonstration.
days.evidence: Two technique cues, an error correction, and an accessibility adaptation.

days.instruction: Discuss how effort, environment, access and recovery change the best choice for portfolio construction.
days.practice: Use the week's case to propose an activity, a lower-intensity alternative and a nonparticipation observation pathway.
days.evidence: Three justified pathways and a brief risk assessment.

days.instruction: Examine a fictional activity log: Session A used an easy effort and adequate rest; Session B used uncomfortable effort without recovery. Compare the decisions rather than body outcomes.
days.practice: Analyze a learner's fictional plan for portfolio construction: it lacks a stop cue and adaptation. Rewrite it to satisfy: Select evidence showing revision rather than just performance.
days.evidence: A revision justified by safety and observable learning evidence.

days.instruction: Synthesize what safe and inclusive learning about portfolio construction requires.
days.practice: Create a brief teach-back, annotated movement plan or accessible explanation; reflect on a misconception.
days.evidence: Portfolio entry with claim, observation, adaptation and next step.

weeks.misconception: More intensity or outperforming classmates always means better learning about portfolio construction.
weeks.correction: Learning is evaluated by informed choices, safe technique, explanation, reflection and documented progress relative to a learner's own context.
weeks.teacherNotes: Check for accessible alternatives and informed consent. Never require disclosure of medical history or body measurements. Model neutral language for portfolio construction.

checks.prompt: A peer says, "More intensity or outperforming classmates always means better learning about portfolio construction." Which response best corrects the reasoning?
options: Treat effort or peer comparison as the main evidence, even when task conditions differ.
Learning is evaluated by informed choices, safe technique, explanation, reflection and documented progress relative to a learner's own context.
Keep the claim without checking the observation, adaptation, or learning objective.
checks.rationale: The correction prioritizes learning evidence and avoids unsupported comparisons or unsafe generalizations.

checks.prompt: The current plan for portfolio construction is missing a clear success criterion. What revision is most useful?
options: Add more activity without deciding what will be observed.
Judge success by effort alone and omit the learning evidence.
Name one observable criterion for "select evidence showing revision rather than just performance", then record what happened and what remains uncertain.
checks.rationale: A clear criterion connects the activity to observable evidence and acknowledges uncertainty.

checks.prompt: A learner cannot use the original movement format for portfolio construction. Which adaptation is strongest?
options: Remove the learner from the task without an alternative.
Require private medical details before offering an adjustment.
Choose a safe accessible demonstration, observation, or explanation that still measures "select evidence showing revision rather than just performance".
checks.rationale: An equivalent accessible pathway preserves the objective without exclusion or unnecessary health disclosure.

checks.prompt: While practicing "select evidence showing revision rather than just performance", a learner notices a new safety concern. What is the best response?
options: Continue unchanged because the plan was already written.
Pause, assess the concern, and choose a safer option or seek appropriate guidance before continuing.
Ask peers to vote on whether a warning sign should be ignored.
checks.rationale: A plan must adapt to new information; safety takes priority over completing a preset task.

checks.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported after a learner completes the five-day sequence for portfolio construction?
options: The learner has mastered every related skill in every setting.
The learner can explain a choice, provide relevant evidence, and identify a limitation or next step.
The learner should use the same activity and difficulty in all future sessions.
checks.rationale: A learning record supports conclusions limited to the observed task; it does not prove universal mastery or a one-size-fits-all plan.

checks.prompt: What should a PE portfolio demonstrate beyond a completed activity?
options: Only the strongest result.
Evidence of learning, reflection, and how the plan or skill changed.
A ranking of classmates.
checks.rationale: A portfolio should show the learning process as well as the outcome.

checks.prompt: Which item is strong evidence of revision?
options: An earlier plan, a reasoned change, and a note explaining the new choice.
Only the final plan with no explanation.
A claim that the learner never made a mistake.
checks.rationale: Revision evidence makes the change and its rationale visible.

checks.prompt: Why should portfolio evidence be dated or identified by week?
options: It helps connect the artifact to the learning sequence and reflection.
Dates guarantee accuracy.
It permits the learner to hide changes.
checks.rationale: Labels make it possible to understand where evidence fits in the course.

checks.prompt: Which portfolio entry best respects privacy?
options: A public ranking of participants.
A classmate's private health record.
A description of the learning decision without unnecessary medical or personal details.
checks.rationale: The portfolio should include only information needed to demonstrate learning.

checks.prompt: A learner has an oral explanation instead of a physical demonstration. What should the portfolio show?
options: How the explanation meets the same stated learning criteria.
Why the learner must receive no credit.
The learner's diagnosis.
checks.rationale: Alternative evidence can be assessed against the same learning target.

checks.prompt: Which artifact is useful for showing critical thinking?
options: A comparison of two plans with reasons for selecting one and noting limitations.
A list of activities copied without comment.
A promise to always choose the hardest task.
checks.rationale: Comparing options and explaining a decision demonstrates reasoning.

checks.prompt: How should a student select artifacts for a portfolio?
options: Include every private detail available.
Choose only the most colorful file.
Choose evidence aligned with the learning outcomes and explain why it is relevant.
checks.rationale: Relevant selection is more useful than unfiltered or decorative evidence.

checks.prompt: What is a reflection meant to explain?
options: What the learner noticed, why a choice was made, and what could change next.
Only whether the learner is good or bad at PE.
How to compare bodies.
checks.rationale: Reflection interprets evidence and informs a next step.

checks.prompt: A portfolio contains conflicting entries from two dates. What should the learner do?
options: Delete the entry that looks less successful.
Check dates and context, preserve the record, and explain the difference if known.
Pretend the difference does not exist.
checks.rationale: Conflicts should be investigated and explained rather than hidden.

checks.prompt: Why include an adaptation in the portfolio?
options: It is private information that must be public.
It automatically lowers the grade.
It documents how the learner accessed the goal and made a reasoned choice.
checks.rationale: Adaptations can be evidence of problem-solving and access-aware planning.

checks.prompt: What is a weakness of a portfolio containing only scores?
options: The portfolio is always invalid.
Scores are never evidence.
It may omit reasoning, process, context, and improvement over time.
checks.rationale: Scores alone often do not show the reasoning or process behind a result.

checks.prompt: Which caption best explains an artifact?
options: This is good because it is good.
This revision changed the route after a safety check and kept the navigation objective.
This proves I am better than everyone.
checks.rationale: A useful caption links the artifact to a specific decision and learning target.

checks.prompt: How can a learner check a portfolio for completeness?
options: Assume any number of entries is enough.
Compare entries against the course criteria and note any missing evidence.
Use only the most recent item.
checks.rationale: A checklist of criteria helps identify gaps before submission.

checks.prompt: What should a portfolio avoid?
options: Unnecessary sensitive information and unsupported claims.
Clear dates and explanations.
Examples of revised decisions.
checks.rationale: Portfolios should be relevant, respectful, and evidence-based.

checks.prompt: Which artifact helps show progress in feedback skills?
options: A list of classmate rankings.
Only a picture of the learner.
A sample of a feedback cue and a later reflection on how it was used.
checks.rationale: Specific feedback evidence can show how the learner translated a cue into action.

checks.prompt: Why is a portfolio stronger when it includes limitations?
options: It shows the learner understands what the evidence can and cannot establish.
Limitations make evidence useless.
A successful portfolio must claim certainty.
checks.rationale: Acknowledging limits is part of careful reasoning.

checks.prompt: A student wants to include a peer's work in their portfolio. What should they consider?
options: Assume all peer work is free to publish.
Permission, privacy, attribution, and whether the peer's work is necessary.
Include private comments without asking.
checks.rationale: Permission and responsible attribution matter when using another person's work.

checks.prompt: Which organization method helps a teacher review the portfolio?
options: Remove the explanations.
Mix everything without headings.
Group evidence by learning target or week with clear labels.
checks.rationale: Organization makes the evidence easier to trace to outcomes.

checks.prompt: How should a learner respond to feedback on a draft portfolio?
options: Review the feedback and revise the selection or explanation where it improves the evidence.
Ignore all feedback automatically.
Replace evidence with claims.
checks.rationale: A portfolio draft is an opportunity to improve clarity and relevance.

checks.prompt: Which portfolio reflection is strongest?
options: Which artifact best shows my decision, what limitation remains, and what I would revise next?
Which classmate had the best body?
How can I guarantee every activity produces the same result?
checks.rationale: A strong reflection identifies evidence, limits, and future improvement.

checks.prompt: What should guide a revision to a personal movement plan?
options: Evidence about the result, a barrier, comfort, access, or changing circumstances.
A desire to make the plan look more difficult.
A classmate's body size.
checks.rationale: Revision should follow relevant evidence and context.

checks.prompt: A plan is repeatedly too long for the learner's schedule. Which change is most reasonable?
options: Keep the same plan and hide missed sessions.
Shorten or rearrange it while preserving the intended goal.
Add more work to compensate.
checks.rationale: A repeated barrier is a reason to make the plan more feasible.

checks.prompt: Why change one major factor at a time when practical?
options: It helps the learner notice which change may have affected the experience.
It guarantees a precise scientific result.
It prevents any learning.
checks.rationale: Focused revisions make it easier to interpret the result, while still acknowledging limits.

checks.prompt: Which is the best revision after a route becomes unsafe?
options: Keep the route because it is in the original plan.
Choose a safer route and record how it still meets the navigation goal.
Remove safety checks.
checks.rationale: Revisions should preserve the objective while responding to safety information.

checks.prompt: How can feedback inform program revision?
options: Use feedback to rank classmates.
Change the entire program without a reason.
Identify a specific cue or barrier, make a reasoned change, and review the result.
checks.rationale: Feedback is most useful when it leads to a concrete, reviewable change.

checks.prompt: A revised plan shows less activity time but better access and consistency. What can be concluded?
options: The revised plan must be worse.
The plan may fit the learner's circumstances better; review the goal and evidence rather than one number alone.
Less time always means no learning.
checks.rationale: Plan quality depends on the learning goal and context, not just one quantity.

checks.prompt: Which revision is justified when equipment is unavailable?
options: Choose a safe alternative that practices the same concept.
Use unsafe equipment to preserve the original plan.
Drop the goal without review.
checks.rationale: Alternative resources can support the same objective when selected appropriately.

checks.prompt: Why should a learner record why a plan was revised?
options: It guarantees the revision works.
It connects the evidence or barrier to the decision.
It prevents further changes.
checks.rationale: A rationale makes the decision traceable and useful for future reflection.

checks.prompt: Which is an overreaction to one unsuccessful practice attempt?
options: Noting the conditions and limitations.
Examining the cue and trying one reasonable change.
Changing every part of the plan without checking what happened.
checks.rationale: One attempt usually provides limited evidence; revisions should be proportionate.

checks.prompt: What should a learner do if the new plan causes pain or other concerning symptoms?
options: Ignore the symptoms until the review date.
Continue because the plan is new.
Stop the activity and seek appropriate guidance before deciding how to proceed.
checks.rationale: Safety concerns take priority over testing a revision.

checks.prompt: How can a teacher assess program revision fairly?
options: Evaluate the reasoning, evidence, and fit of the change to the stated goal.
Reward only higher numerical results.
Require every learner to make the same change.
checks.rationale: The quality of the reasoning matters, and appropriate changes may differ.

checks.prompt: A learner revises a goal after discovering a cost barrier. What should they record?
options: A classmate's financial information.
A claim that cost never matters.
The barrier, the alternative chosen, and how the alternative still supports the purpose.
checks.rationale: The portfolio should connect real constraints to the selected alternative.

checks.prompt: Which data supports a revision to a mobility routine?
options: A note about comfort, control, sequence, and the movement's purpose.
A photo ranking flexibility.
A claim that every person should use the same range.
checks.rationale: Relevant observations are more useful than appearance comparisons.

checks.prompt: What does it mean to evaluate a revision?
options: Never reconsider the plan.
Assume every change succeeds.
Compare what happened with the goal and decide what evidence supports a next step.
checks.rationale: Evaluation checks the revision against the stated target.

checks.prompt: A learner gets conflicting feedback on their plan. What is appropriate?
options: Follow the strictest suggestion automatically.
Clarify the learning goal and compare the reasoning behind each suggestion.
Ignore safety to avoid disagreement.
checks.rationale: Conflicting feedback should be assessed against the objective and safety.

checks.prompt: Which is a useful way to avoid bias when reviewing a plan?
options: Use clear criteria and relevant evidence rather than assumptions about appearance or ability.
Score based on personal popularity.
Assume the first idea was best.
checks.rationale: Explicit criteria make review more consistent and relevant.

checks.prompt: A new plan relies on an inaccessible venue. What should happen?
options: Assume access will somehow work out.
Revise the venue or choose an accessible alternative before relying on the plan.
Tell the learner to manage alone.
checks.rationale: Access barriers should be addressed at the planning stage.

checks.prompt: Which is the best reason to preserve an earlier version of a plan?
options: It prevents anyone from reviewing improvements.
It proves the first version was correct.
It allows the learner to show what changed and why.
checks.rationale: Earlier versions make revision visible and support process reflection.

checks.prompt: How can a student distinguish a revision from a random change?
options: Make several unexplained changes.
Explain what evidence or constraint led to the change and how it fits the goal.
Copy a different plan without checking it.
checks.rationale: A revision responds to evidence and preserves a clear purpose.

checks.prompt: Which reflection best evaluates program revision?
options: What evidence led to my change, what happened afterward, and what remains uncertain?
How can I prevent anyone from changing my plan?
Who was most successful in class?
checks.rationale: A strong review connects rationale and result while recognizing uncertainty.

weeks.focusSkill: Use feedback to change one training decision.

weeks.title: Lifelong activity plan
weeks.essentialQuestion: How can we make a safe, evidence-based decision about lifelong activity plan?
weeks.scenario: A Grade 9 learner is planning a safe, accessible activity involving lifelong activity plan. They have limited time, variable energy, and no specialized equipment.
weeks.model: Worked example (lifelong): A learner wants to practice lifelong activity plan. First identify the specific skill: Plan activity around changing schedules and access. Next compare two feasible options, select one with a clear safety cue, and document the reason. A written, observed, seated or adapted demonstration can meet the same reasoning target.

days.instruction: Introduce lifelong activity plan. Discuss the difference between participation, movement skill and health status. Analyze the case: A Grade 9 learner is planning a safe, accessible activity involving lifelong activity plan. They have limited time, variable energy, and no specialized equipment.
days.practice: Write a three-part safety plan for lifelong activity plan: purpose, feasible option, and stop/modification cue.
days.evidence: A reasoned three-part plan with a specific observable cue.

days.instruction: Teacher models one safe approach to lifelong activity plan and one accessible seated, low-impact, observation or explanation alternative. Compare what each demonstrates.
days.practice: Practice the week's decision with this exact prompt: Plan activity around changing schedules and access. Demonstrate it physically when safe, or explain/annotate an equivalent demonstration.
days.evidence: Two technique cues, an error correction, and an accessibility adaptation.

days.instruction: Discuss how effort, environment, access and recovery change the best choice for lifelong activity plan.
days.practice: Use the week's case to propose an activity, a lower-intensity alternative and a nonparticipation observation pathway.
days.evidence: Three justified pathways and a brief risk assessment.

days.instruction: Examine a fictional activity log: Session A used an easy effort and adequate rest; Session B used uncomfortable effort without recovery. Compare the decisions rather than body outcomes.
days.practice: Analyze a learner's fictional plan for lifelong activity plan: it lacks a stop cue and adaptation. Rewrite it to satisfy: Plan activity around changing schedules and access.
days.evidence: A revision justified by safety and observable learning evidence.

days.instruction: Synthesize what safe and inclusive learning about lifelong activity plan requires.
days.practice: Create a brief teach-back, annotated movement plan or accessible explanation; reflect on a misconception.
days.evidence: Portfolio entry with claim, observation, adaptation and next step.

weeks.misconception: More intensity or outperforming classmates always means better learning about lifelong activity plan.
weeks.correction: Learning is evaluated by informed choices, safe technique, explanation, reflection and documented progress relative to a learner's own context.
weeks.teacherNotes: Check for accessible alternatives and informed consent. Never require disclosure of medical history or body measurements. Model neutral language for lifelong activity plan.

checks.prompt: A learner has limited time and no specialized equipment while preparing for lifelong activity plan. Which next step best supports this week's learning?
options: Copy a classmate's decision without checking the case.
Use completion time as the only measure of learning.
Identify the decision, compare realistic options, and explain the choice using the learning target.
checks.rationale: A contextual decision responds to the actual constraints and makes its reasoning visible; speed or copying is insufficient.

checks.prompt: Which observation gives the strongest evidence of progress on the focus skill "plan activity around changing schedules and access"?
options: A dated before-and-after observation tied to a clear criterion, with limits noted.
A general statement that the learner looked more athletic.
A single score with no description of the task or conditions.
checks.rationale: Relevant, dated evidence tied to a criterion supports a defensible conclusion better than appearance or an unexplained score.

checks.prompt: A peer says, "More intensity or outperforming classmates always means better learning about lifelong activity plan." Which response best corrects the reasoning?
options: Treat effort or peer comparison as the main evidence, even when task conditions differ.
Learning is evaluated by informed choices, safe technique, explanation, reflection and documented progress relative to a learner's own context.
Keep the claim without checking the observation, adaptation, or learning objective.
checks.rationale: The correction prioritizes learning evidence and avoids unsupported comparisons or unsafe generalizations.

checks.prompt: The current plan for lifelong activity plan is missing a clear success criterion. What revision is most useful?
options: Add more activity without deciding what will be observed.
Judge success by effort alone and omit the learning evidence.
Name one observable criterion for "plan activity around changing schedules and access", then record what happened and what remains uncertain.
checks.rationale: A clear criterion connects the activity to observable evidence and acknowledges uncertainty.

checks.prompt: A learner cannot use the original movement format for lifelong activity plan. Which adaptation is strongest?
options: Choose a safe accessible demonstration, observation, or explanation that still measures "plan activity around changing schedules and access".
Remove the learner from the task without an alternative.
Require private medical details before offering an adjustment.
checks.rationale: An equivalent accessible pathway preserves the objective without exclusion or unnecessary health disclosure.

checks.prompt: What makes a lifelong activity plan realistic?
options: It depends on expensive equipment only.
It requires a fixed routine regardless of circumstances.
It can adapt to changing schedules, access, preferences, and resources.
checks.rationale: Lifelong planning must be flexible enough to fit changing circumstances.

checks.prompt: A person changes jobs and has less free time. What should happen to their movement plan?
options: Reconsider the schedule and choose appropriate options that fit the new routine.
Assume the previous schedule must remain unchanged.
Give up all movement indefinitely.
checks.rationale: A life change is a reason to revise the plan, not a reason for blame.

checks.prompt: Which is a useful feature of a long-term activity plan?
options: A rule never to take rest.
Only one option with no alternative.
More than one suitable activity or fallback option.
checks.rationale: Options help the plan remain feasible when conditions change.

checks.prompt: Why can recreation preferences change over time?
options: Changing a preference proves failure.
Preferences must stay the same forever.
Interests, access, social settings, responsibilities, and abilities can change.
checks.rationale: A lifelong plan should support changing interests and constraints.

checks.prompt: Which is an example of an accessible long-term option?
options: A task that requires unsafe conditions.
A program the learner cannot reach or afford.
A suitable low-cost activity in a reachable place with a practical schedule.
checks.rationale: Practical access and resources are part of sustainable planning.

checks.prompt: A learner's preferred activity becomes unavailable. What is a good next step?
options: Identify an alternative that supports a similar purpose and review its fit.
Assume all movement options are gone.
Continue using a closed facility.
checks.rationale: An alternative can preserve the broader aim when a specific option changes.

checks.prompt: Which goal is more sustainable across different life stages?
options: Commit to one exact session plan for all future years.
Keep a flexible menu of activities and periodically review what fits.
Never adapt equipment or timing.
checks.rationale: Flexible planning is more resilient to changing circumstances.

checks.prompt: How should a learner discuss long-term activity with someone who has different preferences?
options: Claim everyone should choose the same activity.
Respect differences and compare options without prescribing one universal routine.
Rank preferences as better or worse.
checks.rationale: Different choices may be suitable for different people and contexts.

checks.prompt: Which factor should be considered when planning activity after graduation?
options: Work or study schedules, transport, cost, access, and community resources.
Only school gym access.
Whether classmates continue the same course.
checks.rationale: A transition plan needs to consider new contexts and available resources.

checks.prompt: A future plan includes an activity that may require instruction. What is appropriate?
options: Begin without understanding the equipment.
Identify where to learn the skill safely before participating independently.
Assume all online advice is accurate.
checks.rationale: Planning for instruction is part of safe participation in unfamiliar activities.

checks.prompt: What does lifelong wellness mean in this course context?
options: Making informed, adaptable decisions about movement and related habits over time.
Maintaining perfect performance forever.
Following a single plan without revision.
checks.rationale: Lifelong wellness emphasizes decision-making, adaptation, and sustainable choices.

checks.prompt: Which is a useful contingency plan?
options: Continue on the same route regardless of conditions.
If the weather or venue changes, use a suitable indoor or alternate option.
Cancel all future activity after one change.
checks.rationale: Fallbacks help a plan respond to predictable barriers.

checks.prompt: Why should a long-term plan include rest and flexibility?
options: Rest always prevents progress.
It supports a realistic approach as needs and schedules vary.
A lifelong plan must be constant.
checks.rationale: Flexibility and rest can be part of maintaining a realistic approach.

checks.prompt: Which evidence helps evaluate a community activity over time?
options: A promise never to stop.
Only its popularity in the first week.
Notes on access, cost, enjoyment, safety, and whether it continues to fit the goal.
checks.rationale: The suitability of an activity can be reviewed as experience accumulates.

checks.prompt: A learner expects future access needs may change. What is a sensible plan?
options: Assume no changes will occur.
Identify activities with adaptable versions and revisit access information when needed.
Require the same physical version indefinitely.
checks.rationale: Anticipating change can make future choices more resilient.

checks.prompt: Which statement avoids an unsupported health promise?
options: This activity is one option I can try and review for fit and enjoyment.
This activity guarantees lifelong health for everyone.
This routine replaces all professional guidance.
checks.rationale: Responsible wellness communication avoids guarantees and recognizes individual differences.

checks.prompt: What information might be useful in a transition resource list?
options: Unverified promises about results.
Trusted activity providers, cost, travel details, accessibility information, and contact methods.
Private records of other participants.
checks.rationale: A practical resource list helps the learner evaluate future options.

checks.prompt: How can a learner define success in a lifelong plan?
options: Use evidence about feasibility, personal goals, access, and adaptation rather than comparison.
Always do more than other people.
Never change the plan.
checks.rationale: Success should reflect the plan's purpose and the learner's circumstances.

checks.prompt: Which is a strong strategy for maintaining an activity habit through disruption?
options: Increase all activity immediately after every disruption.
Treat one missed session as permanent failure.
Choose a small backup option and a way to restart when circumstances improve.
checks.rationale: A backup and a restart plan make the routine more adaptable.

checks.prompt: Which reflection best supports lifelong planning?
options: What options fit my future context, what could change, and how will I reassess?
Which activity should everyone choose?
How do I keep the same plan without considering new information?
checks.rationale: A useful lifelong plan anticipates change and includes review.

weeks.focusSkill: Plan activity around changing schedules and access.

weeks.teacherNotes: Check for accessible alternatives and informed consent. Never require disclosure of medical history or body measurements. Model neutral language for final demonstration and reflection.

checks.prompt: The current plan for final demonstration and reflection is missing a clear success criterion. What revision is most useful?
options: Judge success by effort alone and omit the learning evidence.
Add more activity without deciding what will be observed.
Name one observable criterion for "defend a safe personal plan with evidence and an alternative", then record what happened and what remains uncertain.
checks.rationale: A clear criterion connects the activity to observable evidence and acknowledges uncertainty.

checks.prompt: A learner cannot use the original movement format for final demonstration and reflection. Which adaptation is strongest?
options: Choose a safe accessible demonstration, observation, or explanation that still measures "defend a safe personal plan with evidence and an alternative".
Remove the learner from the task without an alternative.
Require private medical details before offering an adjustment.
checks.rationale: An equivalent accessible pathway preserves the objective without exclusion or unnecessary health disclosure.

checks.prompt: While practicing "defend a safe personal plan with evidence and an alternative", a learner notices a new safety concern. What is the best response?
options: Continue unchanged because the plan was already written.
Pause, assess the concern, and choose a safer option or seek appropriate guidance before continuing.
Ask peers to vote on whether a warning sign should be ignored.
checks.rationale: A plan must adapt to new information; safety takes priority over completing a preset task.

checks.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported after a learner completes the five-day sequence for final demonstration and reflection?
options: The learner has mastered every related skill in every setting.
The learner can explain a choice, provide relevant evidence, and identify a limitation or next step.
The learner should use the same activity and difficulty in all future sessions.
checks.rationale: A learning record supports conclusions limited to the observed task; it does not prove universal mastery or a one-size-fits-all plan.

checks.prompt: During final demonstration and reflection, which plan best applies the week's focus skill: defend a safe personal plan with evidence and an alternative?
options: Choose the hardest version regardless of conditions.
Record only whether the task was finished, without explaining the decision.
Practice the focus skill in a feasible task, explain the choice, and record observable evidence.
checks.rationale: The learner applies defend a safe personal plan with evidence and an alternative by making a feasible, justified choice and pointing to evidence relevant to final demonstration and reflection.

checks.prompt: What should a final PE demonstration or portfolio defense include?
options: Only a claim that the learner performed perfectly.
The goal, evidence, safety decisions, adaptations, and a reasoned reflection.
A ranking of classmates.
checks.rationale: A capstone should show both evidence and the reasoning behind the learner's choices.

checks.prompt: A learner cannot safely perform a planned demonstration. How can they show the learning target?
options: Be required to disclose a diagnosis publicly.
Receive an automatic failure.
Use a suitable adapted demonstration, case analysis, or clear explanation based on the rubric.
checks.rationale: Equivalent evidence can demonstrate the target without forcing unsafe participation or disclosure.

checks.prompt: Which is the strongest defense of a personal movement plan?
options: Explain why the plan fits the goal, constraints, safety cues, and alternative pathways.
Say only that it is the hardest plan.
Copy another plan without explanation.
checks.rationale: A defense links choices to evidence, context, and purpose.

checks.prompt: Why should final reflection include limitations?
options: It cancels all previous learning.
It shows the learner understands what the evidence cannot establish and what could be improved.
A final project must claim certainty.
checks.rationale: Recognizing limitations is part of evidence-based reasoning.

checks.prompt: Which item best demonstrates learning across the course?
options: A photo of the learner.
One final score without context.
An early plan, an informed revision, and a reflection on why the change was made.
checks.rationale: A sequence of evidence can show growth in reasoning and revision.

checks.prompt: How should a learner respond to a rubric criterion they do not understand?
options: Ignore the criterion.
Guess what the teacher wants and hide uncertainty.
Ask for clarification and connect their evidence to the criterion.
checks.rationale: Clarification helps ensure the evidence aligns with the actual learning target.

checks.prompt: What is the purpose of a final evidence review?
options: Check whether each claim is supported and whether the record is complete and relevant.
Make all results appear perfect.
Remove adaptations from the record.
checks.rationale: Evidence review improves alignment, accuracy, and clarity.

checks.prompt: A final plan uses several activities. What should the learner explain?
options: How each activity contributes to the goal and fits the available resources and safety needs.
Only which activity looks most impressive.
Why the activities can never change.
checks.rationale: The plan should explain its structure and feasibility.

checks.prompt: Which final reflection is most defensible?
options: My plan is right for every person.
My evidence supports this choice under these conditions; another context could require a change.
I have no more to learn.
checks.rationale: A defensible conclusion is specific about conditions and acknowledges uncertainty.

checks.prompt: What should the learner do if a source used in the final portfolio is unreliable?
options: Replace it with a more credible source or explain why it cannot support the claim.
Keep it because it agrees with the conclusion.
Remove all citations.
checks.rationale: A final evidence review should address source quality.

checks.prompt: How should teacher feedback be handled before finalizing the portfolio?
options: Change the plan without noting why.
Ignore every comment.
Use relevant feedback to clarify claims or revise the evidence and document the change.
checks.rationale: Feedback can improve accuracy and clarity when applied thoughtfully.

checks.prompt: Which evidence should not be used as the sole basis for awarding PE learning?
options: A reasoned safety decision.
Physical appearance or a single raw performance number without reference to the learning criteria.
An explanation of how an adaptation met the target.
checks.rationale: Assessment should align with explicit learning criteria, not appearance or one isolated metric.

checks.prompt: A student has a strong written explanation but limited practical evidence. What should the teacher do?
options: Lower the grade based on assumptions.
Invent performance evidence.
Use the published rubric and request any needed evidence through an accessible pathway.
checks.rationale: Assessment decisions should use actual evidence and transparent criteria.

checks.prompt: What should be included in a final safety rationale?
options: The relevant hazard or condition, selected action, and why the action was appropriate.
Only a statement that the learner is careful.
A promise that risk does not exist.
checks.rationale: A safety rationale explains the decision rather than claiming perfect safety.

checks.prompt: Why is it helpful to connect a final plan to earlier weekly work?
options: It means no final reflection is needed.
It guarantees a specific transcript grade.
It shows how goals, evidence, and revisions developed over time.
checks.rationale: Connections make the learning process visible across the course.

checks.prompt: Which is an appropriate final demonstration when physical activity would be unsuitable?
options: Perform the unsafe task for evidence.
Analyze a scenario, design a safe plan, and explain the movement principles and adaptations.
Skip all learning criteria.
checks.rationale: Reasoned alternatives can assess knowledge without requiring unsuitable physical activity.

checks.prompt: How should a learner discuss uncertainty in a final defense?
options: Pretend there are no limitations.
Identify what the evidence shows, what remains unknown, and what could be checked next.
Use uncertainty to avoid explaining the evidence.
checks.rationale: Accurate communication distinguishes evidence from assumptions.

checks.prompt: Which portfolio practice protects a classmate's privacy?
options: Use only authorized, necessary peer evidence and remove identifying details when appropriate.
Publish peer comments without consent.
Include another person's health history.
checks.rationale: Privacy and permission matter when portfolio materials involve other people.

checks.prompt: What makes a final activity plan sustainable?
options: It is feasible, adaptable, aligned with the goal, and includes ways to review it.
It uses maximum effort for every session.
It prohibits rest and revision.
checks.rationale: Sustainability depends on fit, adaptability, and meaningful evaluation.

checks.prompt: Which is the best final course reflection?
options: What have I learned about safe choices, accessible movement, evidence, and adapting plans over time?
Who was the best body in class?
Why should a plan never change after graduation?
checks.rationale: The course culminates in transferable reasoning about movement, access, safety, and lifelong planning.

weeks.focusSkill: Defend a safe personal plan with evidence and an alternative.

revision.note: Weeks 9–36 first five items use varied topic-derived prompts covering application, constraints, evidence quality, misconception correction, success criteria, accessibility, safety adaptation, and limits of conclusions. Correct answer positions are balanced.
